data.name: I.F.O
data.detailed_description:
I.F.O is an old school LCD-style shoot'em up game.
You have to shoot UFOs using a classic aircraft and save the animals kidnapped by the aliens.
Let's save the Earth from the aliens! You are the last hero of the world.

Very simple controls - You can rotate aircraft by left & right buttons. and you can dash by pushing both buttons together. That's all.

The mysterious alien power - If you kidnap an alien, your classic airplane gets power up by the mysterious alien power.

Unique weapon & item - You can change weapon while saving the animals kidnapped by the aliens. And you can recover your life at the same time. Depends on the kind of animal, you can earn a heart piece which make your maximum life larger.

Support touch input - On the Tablet PC, you can play game by touching the buttons on the screen directly.

Total Battery is
Gon Lee - Code, Art

and
Title BGM is OTOnoniwa
In game BGM is Skipmore

reviews.review:
I.F.O is a small but distinctive arcade shooter that takes inspiration from the era of dedicated LCD handheld games rather than simply copying the familiar pixel-art style of classic consoles. Developed by Total Battery and published by Turtle Cream, it builds its entire identity around simplicity, quick sessions, and score chasing. The result is an unusual little shooter that can be understood within minutes but becomes considerably more demanding when survival and high scores enter the equation.

The premise is appropriately uncomplicated. Aliens have appeared in flying saucers and are abducting animals, leaving the player to take control of a small aircraft and fight back. There is no elaborate storyline or lengthy introduction to get through. The game quickly places the player into the action, where destroying UFOs, rescuing animals, avoiding danger, and staying alive become the priorities. This direct approach fits the arcade format extremely well because every mechanic exists primarily to keep the action moving.

Movement is one of the more interesting aspects of the design. Rather than giving the player a complicated collection of commands, I.F.O relies on a deliberately restricted control system. The aircraft can turn left and right, while another input combination allows it to dash. It initially feels almost too simple, but those limitations are precisely what make positioning important. Players cannot casually move anywhere they want, so anticipating threats and understanding the aircraft's momentum become increasingly important as enemies crowd the play area.

Combat follows the same philosophy of accessibility combined with gradually increasing pressure. Shooting down UFOs is straightforward, but successful attacks can provide useful power-ups that improve the player's modest aircraft. Rescuing abducted animals introduces another consideration beyond simply destroying everything on screen. As a run develops, the combination of enemies, movement restrictions, power-ups, and rescue opportunities creates a surprisingly busy challenge despite the limited number of basic controls.

The scoring system gives the game most of its replay value. I.F.O is designed around repeated attempts rather than a lengthy campaign filled with narrative checkpoints. Leaderboards encourage players to improve their performance, while achievements provide additional objectives for anyone interested in completing everything. A failed attempt rarely feels like a major loss of progress because another run can begin almost immediately. This makes the game particularly effective for short sessions when there is only enough time for a few attempts.

Its visual presentation is arguably the most memorable element. The graphics imitate the fixed shapes and limited appearance of vintage LCD electronic games, giving characters, aircraft, UFOs, and other objects a deliberately mechanical quality. Instead of treating graphical limitations as something to overcome, the game makes them central to its personality. The restrained presentation is easy to read during hectic moments and gives the entire experience a nostalgic character without relying on conventional 8-bit or 16-bit pixel art.

That same commitment to minimalism also defines the game's biggest limitation. There is not an enormous amount of content or mechanical complexity beneath the surface. Players expecting a large campaign, extensive progression systems, numerous ships, elaborate levels, or a deep upgrade tree may find the experience too narrow. Much of its longevity depends on whether chasing higher scores and improving mastery of the controls remains entertaining. Someone who prefers constant unlocks and new environments will probably exhaust its possibilities sooner than a dedicated arcade enthusiast.

Steam Deck compatibility is listed as Playable rather than Verified. The core gameplay works with the handheld's controls, text is readable, and the game's modest technical demands make it naturally suited to portable sessions. However, some interface prompts may occasionally reference mouse, keyboard, or other controller inputs instead of displaying Steam Deck-specific icons. This prevents it from receiving the completely seamless Verified classification, but it remains a practical game to play on the device.

I.F.O ultimately works because it does not attempt to inflate a deliberately modest concept. It takes the aesthetics of old LCD handhelds, combines them with responsive arcade shooting, unusual movement mechanics, animal rescues, power-ups, achievements, and leaderboard competition, then packages everything into an experience intended for quick replayable sessions. Its limited scope will naturally reduce its appeal for players searching for a substantial campaign, but those who appreciate minimalist arcade games can find a surprisingly engaging challenge underneath its simple appearance.

Rating: 8/10
